'''''Hemerocallis fulva''''', the '''orange day-lily''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=17 October 2014 }}</ref> '''tawny daylily''', '''corn lily''', '''tiger daylily''', '''fulvous daylily''', '''ditch lily''' or '''Fourth of July lily''' (also '''railroad daylily''', '''roadside daylily''', '''outhouse lily''', '''track lily''', and '''wash-house lily'''),{{citation needed|date=July 2017}} is a species of [[daylily]] native to Asia. It is very widely grown as an [[ornamental plant]] in [[temperate climates]] for its showy flowers and ease of cultivation. It is not a true [[lily]] in the genus ''Lilium'', but gets its common name from the superficial similarity of its flowers to ''Lilium'' and from the fact that each flower lasts only one day.
[[File:Orange day-lily in Tashkent Botanical Garden.jpg|thumb|Orange day-lily in Tashkent Botanical Garden]]

==Etymology==
The genus name ''Hemerocallis'' is from {{langx|grc|ἡμεροκαλλές}} {{grc-tr|ἡμεροκαλλές}}, literally, ''beautiful [for a] day'' (from {{langx|grc|ἡμέρα}} {{grc-tr|ἡμέρα}} - ''day'', and {{langx|grc|κάλλος}} {{grc-tr|κάλλος}} - ''beautiful''). In Ancient Greek, it referred to [[martagon lily]] and describes the daily nature of flower opening.

The species name is from {{langx|la|fulva}} meaning ''reddish yellow'' in reference to the flower's color.

==Description==
It is an [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]] growing from [[tuberous root]]s, with stems {{convert|40–150|cm|abbr=off}} tall. The [[leaves]] are linear, {{convert|0.5-1.5|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} long and {{convert|1.5–3|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} broad.<ref name="Elias-2009">{{Cite book |last1=Elias |first1=Thomas S. |title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods |last2=Dykeman |first2=Peter A. |publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9 |location=New York |pages=136 |oclc=244766414 |orig-year=1982 }}</ref> The [[flower]]s are {{convert|5–12|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} across, orange-red, with a pale central line on each [[tepal]]; they are produced from early summer through late autumn on scapes of ten through twenty flowers, with the individual flowers opening successively, each one lasting only one day. Its fruit is a three-valved [[capsule (fruit)|capsule]] {{convert|2–2.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and {{convert|1.2–1.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} broad which splits open at maturity and releases [[seed]]s.<ref name=foc/><ref name=rhs/>

Both [[diploid]] and [[triploid]] forms occur in the wild, but most cultivated plants are triploids which rarely produce seeds and primarily reproduce vegetatively by [[stolon]]s.<ref name=foc /> At least four botanical varieties are recognized, including the typical triploid var. ''fulva'', the diploid, long-flowered var. ''angustifolia'' ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]]: var. ''longituba''), the triploid var. ''Flore Pleno'', which has petaloid stamens, and the evergreen var. ''aurantiaca''.<ref name=foc/>

==Distribution==
Orange daylily is native to Asia from the [[Caucasus]] east through the [[Himalaya]] through China, Japan, and Korea.<ref name=foc>{{eFloras|2|200027676|Hemerocallis fulva }}</ref><ref name=rhs>Huxley, A., ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. Macmillan {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}.</ref><ref name=grin>{{GRIN | accessdate = 1 January 2018 }}</ref><ref>S.K. Czerepanov. Vascular Plants of Russia and Adjacent States (2007)</ref> Orange daylily persists where planted, making them a very good garden plant.

''Hemerocallis fulva'' var. ''fulva'' has [[escaped plant|escaped from cultivation]] across much of the United States and parts of Canada and has become a weedy or [[invasive species]].<ref>{{PLANTS |symbol=HEFU |taxon=USDA Plants Profile for Hemerocallis fulva (orange daylily)(Classified as invasive only by Wisconsin) |access-date=31 May 2018 }}</ref> It persists also where dumped and spreads more or less rapidly by vegetative increase into woods and fields and along roadsides and ditches, hence its common name ditch lily. It forms dense stands that exclude native vegetation, and is often mistaken for a [[native species]].

''Hemerocallis fulva'' is an invasive non-native plant in parts of the United States and is included on lists of plants to avoid planting in some states, including Delaware,<ref>{{Cite web |date=16 July 2024 |title=Delaware Invasive Species Council |url=https://delawareinvasives.net/ |access-date=16 July 2024 |website=Delaware Invasive Species Council }}</ref> Maryland,<ref>{{Cite web |date=22 June 2023 |title=Maryland Invasive Plant List |url=https://mda.maryland.gov/Plants-Pests/ |access-date=22 June 2023 |website=Maryland Department of Agriculture }}</ref> Virginia<ref>{{Cite web |date=22 June 2023 |title=Common Day Lily |url=https://mgnv.org/plants/invasive-plants/common-daylily/ |access-date=22 June 2023 |website=Master Gardeners of Northern Virginia }}</ref> and other mid-Atlantic states.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Common Daylily (Hemerocallis fulva) |url=https://www.invasive.org/alien/pubs/midatlantic/hefu.htm |access-date=22 June 2023 |website=www.invasive.org }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Hemerocallis fulva'' has been cultivated in Europe, and naturalized in many countries there, since at least the 16th century.<ref name="PranceNesbitt2012">{{cite book |author1=Sir Ghillean Prance |author2=Mark Nesbitt |title=The Cultural History of Plants |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=niwsBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA268 |date=12 October 2012 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-95811-4 |pages=268– }}</ref> Several modern cultivars exist which are grown as ornamental plants.<ref name="WiersemaLeón1999">{{cite book |author1=John H. Wiersema |author2=Blanca León |title=World Economic Plants: A Standard Reference |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gZlWfNTm-boC&pg=PA256 |date=26 February 1999 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-0-8493-2119-1 |pages=256– }}</ref> As most of the varieties in cultivation are [[Polyploidy|sterile triploids]], and all spread via subterranean bulb offsets, the most common (and simplest) method of [[Plant propagation|propagation]] is by root- or bulb-division. 

''H. fulva'' are long-lived perennials, and are adaptable to a range of climatic conditions. The species is a vigorous grower in nearly any location, thriving even in difficult areas where other plants do not thrive. The plants grow well in full sun to open shade, and are drought tolerant. ''H. fulva'' is winter hardy to UDSA Zone'' ''4.<ref name="Ani_ko2008">{{cite book |author=Tomasz Ani_ko |title=When Perennials Bloom: An Almanac for Planning and Planting |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ODYpMZXFnSQC&pg=PA247 |date=1 January 2008 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=978-0-88192-887-7 |pages=247– }}</ref>

All parts of ''Hemerocallis'' species are seriously and often fatally toxic to cats and somewhat toxic to dogs (as are all lilies in the "true lily" and "daylily" families). Cats are particularly vulnerable as their grooming behaviour causes them to lick accidentally transferred pollen from their fur.<ref>{{cite web |title=Lovely Lilies and Curious Cats: A Dangerous Combination |date=16 September 2021 |url=https://www.fda.gov/animal-veterinary/animal-health-literacy/lovely-lilies-and-curious-cats-dangerous-combination#:~:text=Lilies%20in%20the%20“true%20lily,the%20water%20in%20a%20vase. |publisher=US Food and Drug Admin }}</ref><ref name=MileKhan06>{{Cite journal |last1=Milewski |first1=Lynn M. |last2=Khan |first2=Safdar A. |date=2006 |title=An overview of potentially life-threatening poisonous plants in dogs and cats |journal=Journal of Veterinary Emergency and Critical Care |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=25–33 |url=https://confluence.cornell.edu/download/attachments/117750764/JVECCS%20Poisonous%20Plants.pdf |access-date=28 July 2022 |doi=10.1111/j.1476-4431.2005.00151.x |s2cid=71027971 |name-list-style=amp }}</ref>

==Uses==
The flowers, leaves, and tubers of ''H. fulva'' are edible.<ref name="PFAF">{{PFAF |access-date=20 November 2018 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Edible Landscaping: Eat Your Environment |url=https://www.homestead.org/food/edible-landscaping-eat-your-environment/ |website=homestead.org |date=26 May 2018 |access-date=20 November 2018 }}</ref> The leaves and shoots can be eaten raw or cooked when very young, lest they become too fibrous. The flower petals and young tubers can also be eaten raw in salads, stir-fried, or otherwise cooked. The petals seem to taste better when cooked, but can also be fried for storing,<ref>{{Cite book |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Skyhorse Publishing]] |author=[[United States Department of the Army]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60239-692-0 |location=New York |pages=51 |oclc=277203364 }}</ref> or dried and used as a thickener in soups or sauces.<ref name="PFAF" /> The cooked flower buds, served with butter, taste like [[Green bean|green beans]] or wax beans.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering |last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-year=1979 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=600 }}</ref> The tubers are a good potato substitute, with a reportedly "nutty" flavor.<ref name="Elias-2009" />
